thread:
alex: Quick RFC follow-up — v4 will switch stop_sequence handling from token-level short-circuiting to post-generation trimming. This matches the new sampler semantics but will break older clients that expect streaming early termination. We need a short compatibility plan (server shim + rollout) so customers streaming with incremental stop behavior don't see regressions.
maria: Ugh, this is going to hit some of the chatbot flows. Can we default to the old behavior if a client sends an opt-in header? e.g. `X-Redwood-Legacy-Stop: incremental`? :thinking:
ryan: I ran a quick perf check in staging with a prototype shim. Results: ~4-6% extra CPU on the streaming path, ~8ms added latency P50 for short responses. Not negligible but doable for tenants that explicitly opt in.
sam: +1 for making it opt-in per-tenant and per-route. Also propose a feature-flagged rollout so we can flip for cohorts. We should avoid being on by default.
beth: Ops questions — how would we express this in config? Route-level override? Tenant-level? We already have per-tenant feature flags and a routing header. Maybe use both: header to opt-in per-request, tenant flag for default. Example: 
```
# tenant config example
compatibility_flags:
  legacy_stop_sequence: true  # tenant default
```
and request header: `X-Redwood-Legacy-Stop: incremental` to override.
alex: That matches my thinking. Important: header must be honored for streaming connections that are long-lived (websockets). The shim will need to intercept streaming frames and map the old "stop-as-soon-as-token-emitted" logic onto post-trimmed outputs. Implementation detail: keep generating but scan tokens as they arrive, if header present then close stream when stop seq detected (even if pattern might later be broken by sampling).
ryan: Implementation note: to avoid double-trimming we should attach a flag to the request context so the post-processor knows not to reapply v4 trimming. Also watch out for KV-cache state across shards if we short-circuit early. I flagged potential edge-case where early termination causes different cache lengths and downstream attention math mismatches in certain optimized kernels.
maria: Could we get away with a middle-ground: emit a small sentinel frame to the client when stop seq is first observed, then finish generation in the backend but stop sending tokens? That reduces kernel mismatch risk but keeps client behavior intact. Thoughts?
sam: That's clever — emit a "stop-signal" frame, let the runtime finish but drop subsequent frames to the client. We need to ensure tokens already sent serve as a coherent prefix; also implement a timeout so backend doesn't run forever for adversarial prompts.
beth: From SRE POV: add a counter metric `compat.legacy_stop.enabled` and `compat.legacy_stop.short_circuited` plus a cpu/latency tag on traces. We'll gate retention to 7d for now.
alex: Rollout plan proposal: 1) implement header + tenant flag 2) enable for internal tenants 3) shadow-mode for 2 weeks (capture differences, no behavior change) 4) opt-in cohort (5% tenants) with observability 5) expand to other cohorts if metrics look good.
sam: Can we also add a deprecation warning header when the client is using the legacy header? `X-Redwood-Warn: legacy-stop-deprecated; planned-removal=2027-09-01` so SDKs can surface this.
ryan: I'll open a small RFC PR with the shim design and perf numbers. Putting the prototype code in `runtime/shims/legacy_stop.py` for review.
beth: deploy-bot: deploy queued for canary infra at 1719451480. :rocket:
deploy-bot: deploy started to canary cluster (canary/3 pods). Logs: `deploy/legacy-stop-shim v1.0`
alex: Thanks — once RFC PR is up please ping #eng-platform and #devex so SDK writers can plan. Also add an API changelog note in the console UI to surface the planned semantics change and opt-in strategy.
